claim: Cardiac lymphatics start reaching the zebrafish heart after the larva-to-juvenile transition at approximately 21-34 days post-fertilization (dpf) in fish size 9-12 mm.
source: The first lymphatic vessels, labeled by the TgBAC(prox1a:KalTA4,UAS:uncTagRFP) (hereafter termed 'prox1a') and Tg(lyve1b:dsRed2) (hereafter termed 'lyve1b') transgenes, are detected in the OFT at ~21–34 days post-fertilization (dpf) (fish size 9–12 mm) (Figure 1a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation using transgenic zebrafish lines and documented in Figure 1a-d.

claim: Large collecting lymphatics in the zebrafish OFT expand during development and cover the entire OFT by approximately 8 weeks post-fertilization (wpf) in fish size 14-24 mm.
source: These large collecting lymphatics expand during the following weeks (Figure 1c,d), until they cover the entire OFT by ~8 weeks post-fertilization (wpf) (fish size 14–24 mm) (Figure 1b) and reach their mature form, which remains stable throughout adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by longitudinal observations documented in multiple figures showing lymphatic expansion over time.

claim: Blind-ended lymphatics arising at the base of the OFT sprout towards the zebrafish ventricle at approximately 12-16 wpf (fish size 25-32 mm) in close proximity to major coronary vessels.
source: It is not until ~12–16 wpf (fish size 25–32 mm), however, that blind-ended lymphatics arising at the base of the OFT sprout towards the ventricle, in close proximity to the major coronary vessels (Figure 1e–h, white arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation and imaging data shown in Figure 1e-h.

claim: Isolated clusters of lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) are detected throughout the zebrafish ventricle that are not connected to the OFT or ventricular lymphatics.
source: At similar stages, we also detected isolated clusters of LECs spread throughout the ventricle, which were not connected to the OFT or ventricular lymphatics (Figure 1e,f,h, blue arrows), as well as a dense lymphatic network associated with the epicardial adipose tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, yellow arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing isolated LEC clusters in Figure 1e,f,h.

claim: Zebrafish cardiac lymphatics lack open connections with the blood vasculature as confirmed by intravascular injection of Qdots 705.
source: As with other lymphatic vessels in zebrafish (Yaniv et al., 2006; Jung et al., 2017), cardiac lymphatics lack open connections with the blood vasculature as confirmed by intravascular injection of Qdots 705 (Figure 1k, arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using Qdot injection and references to prior studies.

claim: Zebrafish cardiac lymphatics express lyve1b, prox1a, flt4, and mrc1a transgenic markers.
source: Examination of transgenic zebrafish with labeled LECs, revealed clear expression of lyve1b (Okuda et al., 2012), prox1a (van Impel et al., 2014), Tg(flt4BAC:mCitrine) (hereafter termed 'flt4') (van Impel et al., 2014), and Tg(mrc1a:EGFP) (hereafter termed 'mrc1a') (Jung et al., 2017), in all cardiac lymphatic subsets (Figure 1f–h, Figure 1—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by transgenic reporter expression data and references to prior characterization studies.

claim: 1-5 cells at the tip of zebrafish ventricular lymphatic vessels are labeled primarily by the flt4 transgene.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that 1–5 cells at the tip of ventricular lymphatic vessels were labeled primarily by the flt4 transgene (Figure 1i, arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing differential transgene expression at vessel tips in Figure 1i.

claim: The main cardiac lymphatics in zebrafish are not labeled by the blood vessel marker Tg(kdrl:nls-mCherry) and arterial-specific marker Tg(flt1_9a_cFos:GFP).
source: Finally, we could verify that the main cardiac lymphatics were not labeled by the blood vessel marker Tg(kdrl:nls-mCherry) (Figure 1j, Figure 1—figure supplement 1e,f) and arterial-specific marker Tg(flt1_9a_cFos:GFP) (Figure 1k), which were clearly detected in coronary arteries and arterial capillaries.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing lack of blood vessel marker expression in lymphatics.

claim: The first lymphatic sprouts reach the zebrafish OFT at 21-28 dpf.
source: Live imaging of the different LEC-transgenic reporters revealed that the first lymphatic sprouts reach the OFT at 21–28 dpf (Figure 2a,b, arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: At 21-28 dpf, no blood vessels are detected in the zebrafish OFT prior to lymphatic sprouting.
source: At this stage, no Tg(flt1_9a_cFos:GFP) or Tg(fli1:EGFP)-labeled blood vessels are detected in the heart (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing absence of blood vessel markers in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Zebrafish OFT lymphatic sprouts originate from four facial lyve1b+ vessels called ventral facial lymphatics (VFLs) that run parallel to the ventral aorta.
source: Surprisingly, we found that these sprouts originated in four facial lyve1b+ vessels that run parallel to the ventral aorta (VA) (Figure 2c,d, yellow arrows) (Isogai et al., 2001) before reaching both sides of the OFT (Figure 2d; white arrows). These vessels, which we named 'ventral facial lymphatic (VFLs)', are also labeled by the prox1a transgene (Figure 2e, arrow) and connect to the lymphatics of the branchial arches (Figure 2c (LAA); e, inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing the origin and trajectory of OFT lymphatics from VFLs, with reference to prior anatomical studies.

claim: The ventral facial lymphatics (VFLs) in zebrafish are devoid of blood flow as reflected by the absence of erythrocytes.
source: The VFLs were devoid of blood flow, as reflected by the absence of Tg(gata1a:dsRed2) labelled erythrocytes (Figure 2f, arrows), which were readily detected in the surrounding aorta and gills.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing absence of erythrocyte markers in VFLs in Figure 2f.

claim: Treatment with the beta-adrenergic antagonist Atenolol results in delayed appearance and impaired branching of zebrafish OFT lymphatics.
source: Moreover, heart-rate attenuation following administration of the ß-blocker Atenolol (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) (Hein et al., 2015) resulted in delayed appearance, and impaired branching of OFT lymphatics (Figure 2g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological treatment and references to prior methodology.

claim: Heart rate peaks during the larva to juvenile transition in zebrafish at approximately 21 dpf.
source: To test this hypothesis, we measured the heart rate of zebrafish between 5–40 days post-fertilization (dpf), and found that it indeed peaks during the larva to juvenile transition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by heart rate measurement data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The pro-lymphangiogenic factor vegfc and chemokines cxcl12a and cxcl12b are upregulated in zebrafish OFTs at stages relevant to lymphatic recruitment.
source: To identify molecular candidates mediating lymphatic recruitment, we analyzed gene expression on isolated OFTs at the relevant stages, and detected clear upregulation of the well-established pro-lymphangiogenic factor vegfc, and of the chemokines cxcl12a, and cxcl12b (Figure 2h).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Zebrafish flt4 mutants display marked defects in OFT lymphatics.
source: We observed marked defects in OFT lymphatics following depletion of the Vegfc receptor, Vegfr3/Flt4 (Figure 2i–k). flt4 mutants bear a truncated form of the Flt4 receptor and were shown to lack a thoracic duct at 5dpf (Kok et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from mutant analysis in Figure 2i-k and references to prior characterization of the mutant.

claim: Lymphatic vessels are almost completely absent from the OFTs of zebrafish flt4-/- hearts.
source: In contrast, lymphatic vessels were almost completely absent from the OFTs of flt4 -/- hearts (Figure 2i–k, white arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from mutant analysis shown in Figure 2i-k.

claim: Loss of one copy of vegfc results in maldeveloped lymphatic vessels and overall reduction of OFT lymphatic coverage in zebrafish vegfc+/- fish.
source: In spite of bearing a wild type (wt) vegfc allele, loss of one copy of this gene resulted in maldeveloped lymphatic vessels and overall reduction of OFT lymphatic coverage in vegfc+/- fish (Figure 2l–n).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data from heterozygous mutant analysis in Figure 2l-n.

claim: Zebrafish vegfd-/- hearts do not display substantial defects in OFT lymphatics at three weeks post-fertilization.
source: vegfd-/- hearts (Figure 2—figure supplement 3d,f) in contrast, did not display any substantial defects in OFT lymphatics (Figure 2o–q) or in the VFL (Figure 2—figure supplement 2e, white arrow) at three wpf, despite of displaying minor defects during early facial lymphatic development (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a–c) (Bower et al., 2017a).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from mutant analysis and references to prior studies on early lymphatic development.

claim: Adult zebrafish cxcr4a-/- hearts display only minor defects in OFT lymphatics.
source: Analysis of adult cxcr4a -/- hearts (Siekmann et al., 2009) carrying the lyve1b transgene revealed only minor defects in OFT lymphatics as compared to wt siblings (Figure 2r–t).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from mutant analysis and references to prior characterization of the mutant line.

claim: Homozygous mutants for the cxcl12b ligand (cxcl12b-/-) do not display noticeable phenotypes in zebrafish OFT lymphatics.
source: Moreover, homozygous mutants for the cxcl12b ligand (cxcl12b-/-) did not display any noticeable phenotypes (Figure 2u–w).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from mutant analysis shown in Figure 2u-w.

claim: Changes in heart rate during larva to juvenile transition modulate zebrafish OFT lymphatic development in a Vegfc/Flt4-dependent manner.
source: Altogether, our results suggest that changes in heart rate during larva to juvenile transition modulate OFT lymphatic development in a Vegfc/Flt4-dependent manner, whereas Cxcr4a/Cxcl12b involvement is restricted to remodeling of the OFT lymphatic plexus.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of multiple experimental results including heart rate measurements, pharmacological treatments, and mutant analyses.

claim: Zebrafish ventricular lymphatics sprout in close proximity to major coronary vessels.
source: Interestingly, we found that ventricular lymphatics sprout in close proximity to the major coronary vessels and continue to grow and branch over the following months (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing spatial relationship between lymphatics and coronary vessels in Figure 3b.

claim: Similar association between developing lymphatics and blood vasculature has been described in the mouse heart.
source: Similar association between developing lymphatics and the blood vasculature has been described in the mouse heart (Klotz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to prior studies in mouse.

claim: Treatment with Phenylhydrazine hydrochloride (PHZ) induces cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and enhanced vascularization in zebrafish.
source: To test whether coronary vessels play an active role in ventricular lymphatic development, we treated juvenile zebrafish with Phenylhydrazine hydrochloride (PHZ), which induces CM hypertrophy and enhanced vascularization (Sun et al., 2009). PHZ treatment starting at ~8 wpf- coinciding with the initial development of the coronary plexus-, resulted in enlarged hearts accompanied by enhanced growth and remodeling of coronary vessels (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PHZ treatment and references to prior methodology.

claim: PHZ treatment results in significantly longer lymphatic vessels in zebrafish ventricles that closely follow major coronary vessels.
source: Interestingly, we also detected significantly longer lymphatic vessels in the ventricles of these animals, which closely followed major coronary vessels (Figure 3c,d), suggesting a possible role for the coronary vasculature in lymphatic vessel growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data from PHZ treatment experiments shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: Conditional over-expression of Vegfaa in zebrafish cardiomyocytes results in increased blood vessel coverage and massive expansion of the lymphatic plexus.
source: To further confirm these results, we induced hypervascularization by conditionally over-expressing Vegfaa in CMs using Tg(cmlc2:CreER);(βactin2:loxP-mTagBFP-STOP-loxP-vegfaa) fish (hereafter termed Vegfaa-OE) (Karra et al., 2018) (Figure 3e–g, insets; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a). Vegfaa-OE was induced at ~7 wpf by administration of 4-hydroxytamoxifen and hearts were analyzed 17 days later. As previously reported (Karra et al., 2018), we detected a significant increase in blood vessel coverage, especially those of small caliber (Figure 3e–g, insets; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), which was accompanied by a massive expansion of the lymphatic plexus (Figure 3e–g), supporting a tight association between blood and lymphatic vessel growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from genetic manipulation and references to prior characterization of the model.

claim: Zebrafish cxcr4a mutant hearts bear an immature coronary plexus lacking stereotypical tree-patterning.
source: In order to understand whether coronary vessels are required for proper ventricular lymphatic sprouting, we first examined hearts of cxcr4a-/- fish, which have previously been reported to fail to develop coronary vasculature (Harrison et al., 2015). Surprisingly, we found that neither blood vessel coverage (Figure 3h–j), nor ventricle size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) was affected in cxcr4a-/- hearts. Instead, the coronary plexus appeared immature, lacked its stereotypic hierarchical pattern and the main arteries that run over the OFT and connect to the gills were severely malformed or absent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d, yellow arrow; e, asterisk).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from mutant analysis and references to prior studies, with new observations contradicting previous reports.

claim: The underdeveloped coronary plexus in zebrafish cxcr4a-/- hearts is associated with severely shorter and less branched ventricular lymphatic sprouts.
source: Interestingly, the underdeveloped coronary plexus observed in cxcr4a -/- hearts was associated with severe ventricular lymphatic abnormalities, characterized by markedly shorter and less branched lymphatic sprouts (Figure 3h–j, white arrow, Figure 3—figure supplement 1g), suggesting that the presence of blood ECs per se, is not sufficient to support lymphatic growth, but rather a mature coronary tree is required.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data from mutant analysis shown in Figure 3h-j and Figure 3—figure supplement 1g.

claim: Zebrafish flt4-/- and vegfc+/- hearts display no significant differences in blood vessel coverage and patterning compared to wild-type.
source: To further investigate the nature of the interaction between coronary vessels and ventricular lymphatics, we assessed hearts of flt4 -/- and vegfc+/- animals (Figure 3k–p). In contrast to cxcr4a-/- hearts, we detected no significant differences in blood vessel coverage and patterning (Figure 3k–p, Figure 3—figure supplement 1h,i) as well as in ventricle size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1j,k) in these animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data from mutant analysis shown in multiple figures.

claim: Ventricular lymphatics are severely affected in zebrafish vegfc+/- hearts and nearly absent in flt4-/- hearts.
source: Yet, ventricular lymphatics were severely affected in vegfc+/- and nearly absent in flt4-/- hearts (Figure 3k–p), indicating that Vegfc/Flt4 signaling is absolutely required for ventricular lymphatic formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from mutant analysis shown in Figure 3k-p.

claim: The increased lymphatic growth observed in Vegfaa-OE zebrafish hearts results from expanded blood vasculature and enhanced Vegfc production, not from direct effect of Vegfaa on LECs.
source: In order to test this hypothesis, we over expressed Vegfaa in vegfc+/ - fish. While the reduced levels of Vegfc did not impede Vegfaa-OE induced cardiomegaly and hypervascularization (Figure 3q–t Figure 3—figure supplement 1l,m), the increase of lymphatic coverage (Figure 3e–g) was abrogated in these animals (Figure 3q–t), supporting the idea that a mature coronary plexus serves as a scaffold for ventricular lymphatic development, in a Vegfc-dependent manner. Moreover, these results demonstrate that the increased lymphatic growth observed in Vegfaa-OE hearts results from the expanded blood vasculature and, most probably, from enhanced Vegfc production, and not from a direct effect of Vegfaa on LECs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from genetic manipulation combining Vegfaa overexpression with vegfc heterozygosity.

claim: Isolated lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) in zebrafish ventricles are labeled by prox1a, lyve1b, mrc1a and flt4 transgenic reporters.
source: Besides the 'regular' lymphatic vessels, the zebrafish ventricle holds an additional population of isolated LECs (Figure 1e,f,h), labeled by the prox1a, lyve1b, mrc1a and flt4 transgenic reporters (Figure 1f,h Figure 4a-d, Figure 4—video 1), and positively stained by Prox1 antibody (Figure 4e, arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data using multiple transgenic reporters and antibody staining.

claim: Isolated lymphatic structures in zebrafish initially appear as single cells at approximately 12-13 wpf (fish size 20-22 mm) and later expand to form isolated capillaries at approximately 16 wpf (fish size 23-28 mm).
source: Light sheet imaging of explanted hearts revealed that these lymphatic structures initially appear as single cells (~12–13 wpf, fish size 20–22 mm), that later on expand to form isolated capillaries (~16 wpf, fish size 23–28 mm) (Figure 4b–d, Figure 4—video 1), through a process that resembles lymph-vasculogenesis (Semo et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by light sheet imaging data and references to prior descriptions of lymph-vasculogenesis.

claim: Isolated LECs in zebrafish hearts lack connections to ventricular lymphatics and the arterial network.
source: While we could not determine the exact source of these isolated LECs, we could confirm the lack of connections to ventricular lymphatics (Figure 1f,h; Figure 4c,f) and/or to the arterial network (Figure 4f, inset) suggesting that they may have a separate origin.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing lack of connections in multiple figures.

claim: Isolated LEC clusters in zebrafish develop normally in cxcr4a-/- hearts.
source: Unlike ventricular lymphatics, the isolated LEC clusters appeared normal in cxcr4a-/- hearts (Figure 4g,h, Figure 3—figure supplement 1e, blue arrows, Figure 4—videos 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data from mutant analysis shown in Figure 4g,h.

claim: Vegfaa-OE and PHZ treatment do not affect the numbers and distribution of isolated LECs in zebrafish hearts.
source: Moreover, while Vegfaa-OE induced precocious sprouting of ventricular lymphatics (Figure 3q,r,t) at ~12.5, when they were still absent from control hearts (Figure 3q,t), no effects were detected in the numbers and/or distribution of the isolated LEC following Vegfaa-OE (Figure 4i) or PHZ treatment (Figure 4j).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data from experimental manipulations shown in Figure 4i,j.

claim: Isolated LECs are completely absent from zebrafish flt4-/- hearts.
source: On the other hand, isolated LECs were completely absent from flt4-/- hearts (Figure 4k,l) and markedly reduced in vegfc+/ - hearts (Figure 4m,n).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data from mutant analysis shown in Figure 4k,l.

claim: Isolated LECs are markedly reduced in zebrafish vegfc+/- hearts.
source: On the other hand, isolated LECs were completely absent from flt4-/- hearts (Figure 4k,l) and markedly reduced in vegfc+/ - hearts (Figure 4m,n).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data from mutant analysis shown in Figure 4m,n.

claim: Distinct lymphatic populations in zebrafish respond differently to the same molecular cues.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that distinct lymphatic populations respond differently to the same molecular cues, as is the case of Cxcl12/Cxcr4 signaling which prevented ventricular lymphatic growth but did not impair the appearance of the isolated LEC clusters.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of multiple experimental results comparing responses of different lymphatic populations to various signaling pathways.

claim: Vegfc/Flt4 signaling is absolutely required for formation of both ventricular lymphatics and isolated LEC clusters in zebrafish.
source: In contrast, Vegfc/Flt4 signaling was absolutely required for formation of both populations, indicating its crucial role as key regulator of lymphatic development.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of mutant analysis data showing effects on both lymphatic populations.

claim: At embryonic day E13.5, coronary vessels are present on the dorsal side of the mouse heart but no PROX1+ LECs are detected.
source: At embryonic day E13.5, coronary vessels were already present in the dorsal side of the heart (Figure 5a, red), but no PROX1+ LECs were detected. CMs were the only PROX1+ cells detected over the ventricle at this stage (Figure 5a, green).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: At E14.5, lymphatic sprouts emanating from the sinus venosus region are visualized on the dorsal aspect of the mouse heart.
source: One day later at E14.5, lymphatic sprouts emanating from the sinus venosus region were clearly visualized on the dorsal aspect of the heart, consistent with previous reports (Klotz et al., 2015) (Figure 5b, white arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data and references to prior studies.

claim: Isolated PROX1+ LECs are detected throughout the surface of the mouse ventricle at E14.5.
source: In addition to these lymphatics with clear vessel morphology, we also detected isolated PROX1+ LECs throughout the surface of the ventricle (Figure 5b, inset, blue arrows), similar to the isolated LECs found in the zebrafish heart (Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5b and comparison to zebrafish data.

claim: Both main lymphatic vessels and isolated LECs in mouse hearts express VE-Cadherin.
source: Both the main lymphatic vessels and the isolated LECs also expressed VE-Cadherin.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data.

claim: Isolated LEC clusters in mouse hearts are positive for both PROX1 and LYVE1 and are not connected to main lymphatic vessels at E15.5.
source: Staining with the lymphatic membrane resident receptor LYVE1 at E15.5, confirmed that these LECs clusters, positive for both PROX1 and LYVE1, were not connected to the main lymphatic vessels (Figure 5c, inset, arrows, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Isolated LEC clusters can be found in mouse hearts at E17.5 but are no longer detected at day P23.
source: Clusters could still be found at E17.5 (Figure 5e, inset, arrows, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b–c, Figure 5—video 1), but were no longer detected at day P23 (Figure 5f).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data at multiple developmental stages shown in Figure 5e,f and supplementary figures.

claim: Ccbe1 mutant mice lack both ventricular sprouts and isolated LECs.
source: Interestingly, similar to flt4 mutant fish, Ccbe1 mutant mice lacked both ventricular sprouts and isolated LECs (Figure 5g,h). Ccbe1 is required for lymphangiogenesis in mice (Bos et al., 2011) and fish (Hogan et al., 2009), acting as a regulator of VEGF-C processing (Jha et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from mutant analysis and references to prior studies on Ccbe1 function.

claim: The requirement for VEGF-C/Vegfr3 signaling in both cardiac lymphatic populations is evolutionarily conserved.
source: Thus, the requirement for VEGF-C/Vegfr3 signaling in both cardiac lymphatic populations is evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on comparison of mutant phenotypes in zebrafish and mouse.

claim: PROX1+ LECs in mouse hearts are not labeled by AplnCreERT2 when induced at E12.5 and analyzed at E14.5.
source: AplnCreERT2 mice were crossed to the Cre-dependent ﬂuorescent reporter ROSA26mTmG/+ (Muzumdar et al., 2007) and Cre-mediated recombination was induced by Tamoxifen administration at day E12.5, after the coronary vasculature has formed, but prior to the appearance of lymphatics over the ventricle. Staining with PROX1 and the EC-specific ERG antibodies at E14.5 rendered no PROX1+ cells that were labeled also by the mTmG reporter (Figure 5j).
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data and references to prior characterization of reporter lines.

claim: PROX1+ LECs in mouse hearts are not labeled by ApjCreERT2 when dosed at E12.5 and analyzed at E14.5.
source: This result was also obtained with another Cre that labeled coronary vessels when induced at later stages, ApjCreERT2 dosed at E12.5 (Figure 5k, inset), further confirming that LECs do not originate from the local coronary vasculature, as previously reported (Angeli and Harvey, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data and references to prior studies.

claim: PROX1+ LECs in mouse hearts are not labeled by BmxCreERT2 when induced at E8.5 and analyzed at E15.5.
source: BmxCreERT2 mice were crossed to ROSA26TdTom/+ and Cre-mediated recombination was induced at E8.5. Hearts were harvested at day E15.5 and stained with antibodies against PROX1 and ERG. Despite almost complete endocardial recombination (data not shown), no PROX1+;TdTom+ cells were detected on the surface of the ventricle (Figure 5l, insets), suggesting no significant contribution of the endocardium or embryonic arteries to cardiac lymphatics.
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 5l.

claim: APJCreERT2 lineage labeling when induced at E9.5 and E10.5 results in labeling of a portion of lymphatic vessels and isolated clusters on both dorsal and ventral aspects of the mouse heart at E15.5.
source: Finally, we turned back to APJCreERT2 mice (Chen et al., 2014b), but this time induced labeling at E9.5 and E10.5 to specifically mark the major embryonic veins (SV and CCV) (Chen et al., 2014b) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d,e). Hearts were harvested at day E15.5 and stained as described above. This manipulation resulted in lineage labeling of a portion of the lymphatic vessels and isolated clusters on both the dorsal and ventral aspects of the heart (Figure 5m–o), suggesting that these LECs arose from an early venous source.
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data and references to prior characterization of the Cre line.

claim: The relative incidence of PROX1+/mTmG+ LECs on the dorsal side of the mouse heart at E15.5 is 25% within lymphatic vessels and 21% in isolated clusters when APJCreERT2 is dosed at E9.5/10.5.
source: However, the relative incidence of PROX1+/mTmG+ LECs on the dorsal side of the heart was 25% within lymphatic vessels and 21% in the isolated clusters (Figure 5m).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of lineage tracing data shown in Figure 5m.

claim: The relative incidence of PROX1+/mTmG+ LECs on the ventral side of the mouse heart at E15.5 is 35% within lymphatic vessels and 17% in isolated clusters when APJCreERT2 is dosed at E9.5/10.5.
source: Similar labeling was detected on the ventral side (Figure 5n), with 35% PROX1+/mTmG+ cells within lymphatic vessels and 17% in the isolated clusters (Figure 5o).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of lineage tracing data shown in Figure 5n,o.

claim: Both ventricular lymphatics and isolated LECs in mouse hearts are only partially derived from the APJ+ lineage.
source: These data suggest that both ventricular lymphatics and isolated LECs are only partially derived from the APJ+ lineage.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of lineage tracing quantification data.

claim: Mammalian cardiac lymphatics form by both sprouting lymphangiogenesis and coalescence of isolated LECs (lymph-vasculogenesis).
source: Taken together, our results show that mammalian cardiac lymphatics form by both sprouting lymphangiogenesis and coalescence of isolated LECs (lymph-vasculogenesis).
evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of multiple imaging and lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Neither the local coronary vasculature nor the endocardium contribute to different cardiac lymphatic subsets in mouse based on lineage-tracing strategies.
source: Using multiple lineage-tracing strategies, we show that neither the local coronary vasculature nor the endocardium, contribute to the different cardiac lymphatic subsets.
evidence: The claim is based on multiple lineage tracing experiments using different Cre lines.

claim: Prox1a+ sprouts and new prox1a+ isolated LECs are the first to be detected in the zebrafish injured area as early as approximately 40 hours post cryoinjury (hpci).
source: Notably, we found that prox1a+ sprouts (Figure 6b,c, white arrows), as well as new prox1a+ isolated LECs (Figure 6b,c, yellow arrows) were the first to be detected in the injured area, as early as at ~40 hpci.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from injury experiments shown in Figure 6b,c.

claim: The large majority of lymphatics in the zebrafish injured area between 40 hpci-14 dpci are not connected to large collecting lymphatics of the OFT or to ventricular lymphatics.
source: As a whole, the large majority of lymphatics in the injured area between 40 hpci-14 dpci, were not connected to large collecting lymphatics of the OFT, or to ventricular lymphatics (Figure 6d–i, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b,d,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from multiple time points post-injury shown in Figure 6d-i and supplementary figures.

claim: Injury-specific LEC clusters in zebrafish are highly heterogeneous both in morphology and gene expression.
source: While we could not determine the origins of the injury-specific LEC clusters, which did not appear in sham operated hearts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c,e,g), they were highly heterogeneous both in morphology and gene expression. We could detect cells expressing combinations of LEC markers, such as prox1a and flt4 (Figure 6f, inset, white arrow, Figure 6—video 1), as well as cells expressing prox1a (Figure 6f) or flt4 only (Figure 6f, inset, blue arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing variable marker expression in injury-induced LECs.

claim: Isolated LECs in the zebrafish injured area develop into long sprouts that continue growing throughout the regenerative phase and can be detected even after 2 months post cryoinjury.
source: Interestingly, isolated LECs in the injured area developed into long sprouts (Figure 6h–j, inset, Figure 6—video 3), which continued growing throughout the regenerative phase and could be detected even after 2 months pci (Figure 6l,m, Figure 6—figure supplement 1g,h, Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data at multiple time points post-injury shown in multiple figures.

claim: OFT-derived ventricular lymphatics reach the zebrafish regenerating area at approximately 1-3 weeks post cryoinjury, mostly following their own damage.
source: Contrary to the rapid lymph-vasculogenic response, OFT-derived ventricular lymphatics reached the regenerating area only at ~1–3 weeks pci (Figure 6j, arrows), mostly following their own-damage, as lymphatic vessels that were remote from the injury site, did not respond at all (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data at different time points post-injury shown in Figure 6j.

claim: Ventricular lymphatics and isolated lymphatic clusters are nearly absent in the vicinity and within the injured area of approximately 1 month post-cryoinjury flt4-/- and vegfc+/- zebrafish hearts.
source: We then asked whether the same cues controlling the development of cardiac lymphatics are reactivated during injury. In line with the reduction in ventricular lymphatics (Figure 3m–p) and isolated lymphatic clusters (Figure 4j–m) observed in flt4 -/- and vegfc+/- hearts, these were nearly absent in the vicinity, as well as within the injured area of ~1 month post-cryoinjury (mpci) mutant hearts (Figure 7a–f, arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from injury experiments in mutant fish shown in Figure 7a-f.

claim: At approximately 2 months post-cryoinjury, when an extensive lymphatic network covers the injury in wild-type zebrafish hearts, vegfc+/- hearts remain largely devoid of lymphatic vessels.
source: Even at ~2 mpci, when an extensive lymphatic network covered the injury in wt hearts, vegfc+/- hearts remained largely devoid of lymphatic vessels (Figure 7g–i, arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from injury experiments in mutant fish at later time points shown in Figure 7g-i.

claim: The scar area is increased in injured zebrafish flt4-/- and vegfc+/- hearts.
source: In line with the impaired post-injury neo-lymphangiogenesis (Figure 7a–i), the scar area was increased in injured flt4 -/- and vegfc+/- hearts (Figure 7j–o, arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis and quantification data shown in Figure 7j-o.

claim: In control zebrafish hearts, the fibrotic scar is mostly resolved by approximately 1 month post-cryoinjury and replaced by new muscle tissue, while flt4-/- hearts display a prominent scar.
source: Acid Fuchsin Orange-G (AFOG) staining of heart sections showed that while in control hearts the fibrotic scar was mostly resolved by ~1 mpci and replaced by new muscle tissue, flt4 -/- hearts displayed a prominent scar composed of a collagenous core and a thin layer of fibrin at the border of the wound (Figure 7j–l, arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological staining data shown in Figure 7j-l.

claim: The scar is not resolved in zebrafish vegfc+/- hearts even at approximately 2 months post-cryoinjury.
source: Similarly, the scar was not resolved in vegfc+/- hearts even at ~2 mpci (Figure 7m–o, arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological staining data shown in Figure 7m-o.

claim: Isolated lymphatic clusters are normally detected in the injured area of zebrafish cxcr4a-/- hearts at 29 days post-cryoinjury.
source: In contrast to these results, isolated lymphatic clusters, which develop normally in cxcr4-/- hearts (Figure 4h–i), could be readily detected following injury as well (Figure 7p–r), suggesting that similar programs control lymphatic growth during development and repair.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from injury experiments in mutant fish shown in Figure 7p-r.

claim: Scar area is increased in zebrafish cxcr4a-/- mutant hearts at 77 days post-cryoinjury.
source: Nevertheless, scar area was increased in cxcr4-/- mutant hearts at 77 dpci (Figure 7s–u, arrow), supporting previous studies suggesting a cell-autonomous requirement of Cxcl12/Cxcr4 signaling for CM and/or coronary migration (Harrison et al., 2015; Itou et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis data and references to prior studies on Cxcl12/Cxcr4 function.

claim: The cardiac lymphatic vasculature is composed of distinct subsets that respond differently to lymphangiogenic cues and display unique behaviors during cardiac injury and regeneration.
source: We demonstrate that the cardiac lymphatic vasculature is composed of distinct subsets, which respond differently to lymphangiogenic cues and display unique behaviors during cardiac injury and regeneration.
evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of multiple experimental results comparing different lymphatic populations.

claim: Cardiac injury induces de novo formation of lymphatics through a process reminiscent of lymph-vasculogenesis rather than sprouting lymphangiogenesis.
source: Our results suggest that cardiac injury induces the de novo formation of lymphatics, through a process reminiscent of lymph-vasculogenesis rather than sprouting lymphangiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of imaging data showing isolated LEC formation and coalescence after injury.

claim: Neo-lymphangiogenesis following cardiac injury is necessary for proper scar resolution and cardiac regeneration in zebrafish.
source: Finally, our results indicate that neo-lymphangiogenesis following cardiac injury is necessary for proper scar resolution and cardiac regeneration.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of mutant injury experiments showing impaired regeneration when lymphangiogenesis is blocked.

claim: Lymphatic vessels are required for cardiac regeneration in zebrafish as mutants lacking lymphatics display severely impaired regeneration capabilities.
source: Finally, we show that lymphatic vessels are required for cardiac regeneration in zebrafish as mutants lacking lymphatics display severely impaired regeneration capabilities.
evidence: The claim is supported by injury experiments in flt4 and vegfc mutants showing impaired regeneration.

claim: In zebrafish, the OFT lymphatics along with their derived ventricular lymphatics originate in the VFL, a late forming facial lymphatic vessel.
source: Our analyses of the cellular origins of cardiac lymphatics in zebrafish and mice provide novel insights into the ontogeny of this system. We find that in zebrafish, the OFT lymphatics along with their derived ventricular lymphatics, originate in the VFL (Figure 2), a late forming facial lymphatic vessel.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of imaging data showing the developmental origin of OFT lymphatics.

claim: The zebrafish facial lymphatic network forms from three progenitor populations: two of venous origins (CCV and PHS) and one angioblast-derived.
source: Interestingly, the zebrafish facial lymphatic network itself has recently been shown to form from three progenitor populations. Two of them are of venous origins (CCV and PHS) while the third one is angioblast-derived, and contributes not only to facial lymphatics but also to the hypobranchial artery (Eng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a recent study on facial lymphatic origins.

claim: A population of Isl1-expressing cardiopharyngeal mesoderm (CPM) progenitors contribute LECs to the ventral side of the ventricles and the OFT in mice.
source: This idea, receives further support from recent lineage-tracing experiments in mice revealing that a population of Isl1-expressing CPM progenitors contribute LECs to the ventral side of the ventricles and the OFT (Maruyama et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to recent lineage tracing studies in mouse.

claim: The majority of mouse cardiac lymphatics (78%) originate from TIE2+ endothelial cells that emerge from the common cardinal vein (CCV) and migrate toward the heart.
source: The majority of mouse cardiac lymphatics (78%) has been shown to originate from TIE2+ ECs, which emerge from the common cardinal vein (CCV) and migrate toward the heart (Klotz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to prior lineage tracing studies.

claim: A contribution from hemogenic endothelium to mouse cardiac lymphatics has been proposed, though the exact identity of these cells remains controversial.
source: Additionally, a contribution from the hemogenic endothelium has also been proposed, albeit the exact identity of these cells has remained controversial (Klotz et al., 2015; Ulvmar and Mäkinen, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to prior studies discussing hemogenic endothelium contribution.

claim: Individual cardiac lymphatic vessels in mice contain cells from both TIE2+ and hemogenic endothelium origins, making cardiac lymphatics a mosaic of different sources.
source: Individual vessels contained cells from both origins, making cardiac lymphatics a mosaic of different sources.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on prior lineage tracing studies showing mixed origins.

claim: Isolated LEC clusters in mouse hearts are often found in close proximity to developing coronary vessels.
source: Since these LEC clusters are often found in close proximity to the developing coronary vessels (Figure 5b,d), a feature that was also evident in the zebrafish heart (Figure 4g), we decided to investigate whether they originate from the local vasculature (i.e. coronary vessels).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging observations in both mouse and zebrafish.

claim: Experimental approaches aimed at boosting lymphangiogenesis following myocardial infarction in mice promote healing of the heart.
source: Experimental approaches aimed at boosting lymphangiogenesis following myocardial infarction in mice, were shown to promote healing of the heart.
evidence: The claim is supported by references to prior therapeutic studies.

claim: Pro-lymphangiogenic treatments in mice have been shown to promote healing of the heart after myocardial infarction by reducing fluid retention and improving inflammatory cell clearance.
source: In recent years, there has been growing interest in the role of the lymphatic system in this process, as pro-lymphangiogenic treatments in mice have been shown to promote healing of the heart after MI by reducing fluid retention and improving inflammatory cell clearance (Klotz et al., 2015; Vuorio et al., 2017; Henri et al., 2016; Ishikawa et al., 2007; Vieira et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to multiple prior therapeutic studies.

claim: Exogenous supply of VEGF-C improves cardiac function after myocardial infarction in mice.
source: Moreover, exogenous supply of VEGF-C has been shown to improve cardiac function after MI in mice (Klotz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a prior therapeutic study.

claim: Zebrafish exhibit a remarkable capacity to regenerate their hearts.
source: Zebrafish, unlike mammals, exhibit a remarkable capacity to regenerate their hearts (González-Rosa et al., 2017), making it an ideal model to study the origins and functions of the lymphatic endothelium following cardiac injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to prior studies and established scientific knowledge about zebrafish regeneration.

claim: Two distinct lymphatic populations are identified in the zebrafish heart: one forming through sprouting lymphangiogenesis and a second one established through coalescence of isolated LEC clusters.
source: Our results identify two distinct lymphatic populations in the zebrafish heart: one forming through sprouting lymphangiogenesis, and a second one, established through coalescence of isolated LEC clusters.
evidence: The claim is a summary of imaging data showing two different mechanisms of lymphatic formation.

claim: Cardiac lymphatics in zebrafish and mouse differ in their response to signaling cues.
source: Interestingly, these cardiac lymphatics differ in their response to signaling cues.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of mutant analysis data showing differential responses to various signaling pathways.

claim: Similar LEC populations to those in zebrafish are present in the mouse heart, suggesting that mechanisms underlying cardiac lymphatic development are evolutionarily conserved.
source: We further demonstrate the presence of similar LEC populations in the mouse heart, suggesting that the mechanisms underlying cardiac lymphatic development are evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on comparative imaging data in zebrafish and mouse.

claim: Not all lymphatics respond equally to cardiac injury in zebrafish.
source: Finally, we address the behavior of LECs following cardiac injury in zebrafish, and show that not all lymphatics respond equally to injury, and that coalescence of isolated LECs represents the main mechanism of lymphatic growth following acute cardiac damage.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of injury experiment data showing differential responses of lymphatic populations.

claim: Coalescence of isolated LECs represents the main mechanism of lymphatic growth following acute cardiac damage in zebrafish.
source: Finally, we address the behavior of LECs following cardiac injury in zebrafish, and show that not all lymphatics respond equally to injury, and that coalescence of isolated LECs represents the main mechanism of lymphatic growth following acute cardiac damage.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of injury experiment imaging data.

claim: In the mouse, LECs enter the heart on the ventral side along the outflow tract (OFT) at approximately embryonic day 12.5 (E12.5).
source: In the mouse for instance, LECs were shown to enter the heart on the ventral side along the outﬂow tract (OFT) at approximately embryonic day 12.5 (E12.5), and later emerge on the dorsal side near the sinus venosus at E14.5.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: In the mouse, LECs emerge on the dorsal side of the heart near the sinus venosus at E14.5.
source: In the mouse for instance, LECs were shown to enter the heart on the ventral side along the outﬂow tract (OFT) at approximately embryonic day 12.5 (E12.5), and later emerge on the dorsal side near the sinus venosus at E14.5.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Mouse cardiac lymphatic development occurs in response to VEGF-C expressed in the OFT mesenchyme and cardiac epicardium.
source: This is in response to VEGF-C expressed in the OFT mesenchyme and cardiac epicardium (Klotz et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to prior studies on VEGF-C expression.

claim: From E14.5, LYVE1/PROX1/VEGFR3-expressing lymphatics sprout at the surface of the mouse ventricle expanding from the base toward the apex.
source: From E14.5, LYVE1/PROX1/VEGFR3-expressing lymphatics sprout at the surface of the ventricle expanding from the base toward the apex, and reaching full maturity at postnatal day 15 (P15) (Flaht-Zabost et al., 2014; Angeli and Harvey, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to prior developmental studies.

claim: Mouse cardiac lymphatics reach full maturity at postnatal day 15 (P15).
source: From E14.5, LYVE1/PROX1/VEGFR3-expressing lymphatics sprout at the surface of the ventricle expanding from the base toward the apex, and reaching full maturity at postnatal day 15 (P15) (Flaht-Zabost et al., 2014; Angeli and Harvey, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to prior developmental studies.

claim: The embryonic origins of lymphatic vessels have been debated for over a century, with a model claiming a venous origin for the lymphatic endothelium being predominant.
source: The embryonic origins of lymphatic vessels have been debated for over a century, with a model claiming a venous origin for the lymphatic endothelium being predominant (Semo et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a review discussing historical perspectives and established knowledge.

claim: Recent work in zebrafish and mouse has uncovered additional surprising sources for lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) during embryonic development.
source: However, recent work in zebrafish and mouse has uncovered additional surprising sources for lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) during embryonic development (Nicenboim et al., 2015; Martinez-Corral et al., 2015; Stanczuk et al., 2015; Mahadevan et al., 2014; Klotz et al., 2015; Pichol-Thievend et al., 2018; Stone and Stainier, 2019; Eng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to multiple recent studies.

claim: Additional sources for LECs during embryonic development include vein resident angioblasts in the zebrafish trunk.
source: These include among others, vein resident angioblasts in the zebrafish trunk (Nicenboim et al., 2015), c-kit+ cells in the mouse mesentery (Stanczuk et al., 2015), VavCre-derived yolk sac hemogenic endothelium (Klotz et al., 2015), and the local capillary plexus in the skin (Pichol-Thievend et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a specific prior study.

claim: Additional sources for LECs during embryonic development include c-kit+ cells in the mouse mesentery.
source: These include among others, vein resident angioblasts in the zebrafish trunk (Nicenboim et al., 2015), c-kit+ cells in the mouse mesentery (Stanczuk et al., 2015), VavCre-derived yolk sac hemogenic endothelium (Klotz et al., 2015), and the local capillary plexus in the skin (Pichol-Thievend et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a specific prior study.

claim: Additional sources for LECs during embryonic development include VavCre-derived yolk sac hemogenic endothelium.
source: These include among others, vein resident angioblasts in the zebrafish trunk (Nicenboim et al., 2015), c-kit+ cells in the mouse mesentery (Stanczuk et al., 2015), VavCre-derived yolk sac hemogenic endothelium (Klotz et al., 2015), and the local capillary plexus in the skin (Pichol-Thievend et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a specific prior study.

claim: Additional sources for LECs during embryonic development include the local capillary plexus in the skin.
source: These include among others, vein resident angioblasts in the zebrafish trunk (Nicenboim et al., 2015), c-kit+ cells in the mouse mesentery (Stanczuk et al., 2015), VavCre-derived yolk sac hemogenic endothelium (Klotz et al., 2015), and the local capillary plexus in the skin (Pichol-Thievend et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a specific prior study.

claim: The heart contains a dense network of lymphatic vessels.
source: As most organs in the body, the heart contains a dense network of lymphatic vessels (Klotz et al., 2015; Johnson and Blake, 1966).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to prior anatomical studies and established knowledge.

claim: Normal cardiac function relies on the cardiac lymphatic system for controlling myocardial fluid homeostasis, lipid transport, and the immune response.
source: Normal cardiac function relies on the cardiac lymphatic system for controlling myocardial fluid homeostasis, lipid transport, and the immune response (Brakenhielm and Alitalo, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a review and established knowledge about lymphatic function.

claim: The existence of cardiac lymphatics was reported in the 17th century.
source: While the existence of cardiac lymphatics was reported already in the 17th century (Rudbeck, 1653), only recently have data emerged describing their development and cellular origins in mammals (Klotz et al., 2015; Stone and Stainier, 2019; Flaht-Zabost et al., 2014; Norman and Riley, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a historical source.

claim: Acute myocardial infarction (MI) is one of the most common cardiac pathologies and a leading cause of death worldwide.
source: Acute myocardial infarction (MI) is one of the most common cardiac pathologies and a leading cause of death worldwide.
evidence: The claim is based on established medical and epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Following myocardial infarction in mammals, massive loss of cardiomyocytes combined with limited regenerative capacity of the myocardium result in the formation of a collagen-based scar leading to reduced cardiac function.
source: Following MI in mammals, massive loss of cardiomyocytes (CMs), combined with limited regenerative capacity of the myocardium result in the formation of a collagen-based scar leading to reduced cardiac function.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mammalian cardiac pathophysiology.

claim: In contrast to the zebrafish systemic lymphatic vasculature which develops within the first days of embryonic development, cardiac lymphatics start reaching the heart only after the larva-to-juvenile transition.
source: In contrast to the zebrafish systemic lymphatic vasculature, which develops within the first days of embryonic development (Nicenboim et al., 2015; Yaniv et al., 2006), we find that cardiac lymphatics start reaching the heart only after the larva-to-juvenile transition (Parichy et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to prior studies on systemic lymphatic development and current observations.

claim: Recruitment of isolated LECs during wound healing in adult mouse skin later interconnect through a process reminiscent of lymph-vasculogenesis.
source: In similar fashion, recruitment of isolated LECs was shown to take place during wound healing in the adult mouse skin, which later interconnect through a process reminiscent of lymph-vasculogenesis (Boardman and Swartz, 2003; Rutkowski et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to prior studies on wound healing.

claim: At the periphery of skin wounds, lymphangiogenesis occurs by sprouting of pre-existing lymphatic vessels.
source: In contrast, at the periphery of the wound, lymphangiogenesis occurs by sprouting of pre-existing lymphatic vessels (Paavonen et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a prior study on wound healing.
